questions.question: Use particles to explain what happens when a sugar grain dissolves in water.
questions.expected_answer: The sugar grain is made of particles packed tightly together. Water particles crowd around the grain, are attracted to the sugar particles and pull them away, layer by layer, until the grain is gone. The sugar particles then spread out into the spaces between the water particles.

questions.question: Why is a solution uniform and clear, and why doesn't the solute settle?
questions.expected_answer: The moving water particles knock the solute particles about until they are spread evenly all through the liquid, so every part has the same amount of solute, which makes the solution uniform. The dissolved particles are too small to see and spread too thinly to block light, so the solution is clear. They are kept moving by the water particles, so they never settle.

questions.question: What is the difference between dissolving and melting? Give an example of each.
questions.expected_answer: Melting happens to one substance on its own when it is heated, such as ice turning into water or butter melting in a pan. Dissolving needs two substances, a solute and a solvent: the solvent particles pull the solute particles apart and they spread between them, such as sugar dissolving in tea, which can happen even without heat.
